L7@P0: Abstract
L8@P0: In his Ph.D. thesis, Ira Gessel proved a reciprocity formula for noncommutative
L9@P0: symmetric functions which enables one to count words and permutations with restrictions on the lengths of their increasing runs. We generalize Gessel’s theorem to allow
L10@P0: for a much wider variety of restrictions on increasing run lengths, and use it to complete
L11@P0: the enumeration of permutations with parity restrictions on peaks and valleys, and to
L12@P0: give a systematic method for obtaining generating functions for permutation statistics
L13@P0: that are expressible in terms of increasing runs. Our methods can also be used to obtain
L14@P0: analogous results for alternating runs in permutations.
L15@P0: Keywords: permutations, increasing runs, peaks, valleys, noncommutative symmetric functions
L16@P0: 1. Introduction
L17@P0: Given a set A, let A∗ be the set of all finite sequences of elements of A, including the empty
L18@P0: sequence. We call A an alphabet, the elements of A letters, A∗the free monoid on A,
L19@P0: 1 and
L20@P0: the elements of A∗ words. If we refer to words without specifying an alphabet, then we take
L21@P0: the alphabet to be P, the set of positive integers. Suppose that our alphabet A is a totally
L22@P0: ordered set, such as P. Then every word in A∗can be uniquely decomposed into a sequence
L23@P0: of maximal weakly increasing consecutive subsequences, which we call increasing runs. For
L24@P0: example, the increasing runs of 2142353 are 2, 14, 235, and 3. The notion of increasing runs
L25@P0: clearly extends to permutations as well.
L26@P0: As part of his 1977 Ph.D. thesis, Gessel proved a very general identity involving noncommutative symmetric functions [6, Theorem 5.2] from which we can obtain many generating
L27@P0: functions for words and permutations with restrictions on the lengths of their increasing runs.
L28@P0: We call this result the “run theorem”. In this paper, we present a generalization of Gessel’s
L29@P0: run theorem that will enable us to count words and permutations with an even wider variety

L35@P1: The organization of this paper is as follows. In Section 2, we introduce some preliminary
L36@P1: definitions, state Gessel’s run theorem, and present our generalization of the run theorem.
L37@P1: In Sections 3 and 4, we present two separate applications of the generalized run theorem to
L38@P1: permutation enumeration.
L39@P1: Let π = π1π2 · · · πn be a permutation in Sn, the set of permutations of [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n}
L40@P1: (or more generally, any sequence of n distinct integers); such permutations are called npermutations. We say that i is a peak of π if πi−1 < πi > πi+1 and that i is a valley of π if
L41@P1: πi−1 > πi < πi+1. For example, given π = 5736214, its peaks are 2 and 4, and its valleys are
L42@P1: 3 and 6.
